steps.body: Make the radical a **function**: f(x) = √x. It starts at the origin, rises forever, but slower and slower — a parabola lying on its side (just the top half). Inputs can't be negative and outputs never are: **domain x ≥ 0, range y ≥ 0**.

commonErrors.feedback: √x is not x/2 — it asks what number SQUARES to 49: 7.
That squares 49 — the square root goes the other way: 7.

steps.body: Why no negative inputs? √(−4) isn't a real number (that's i's territory, from complex numbers). And why no negative outputs? The √ symbol means the **principal** (nonnegative) root: √9 is 3, never −3. The graph lives entirely in the first quadrant.

explanationVariants: As a FUNCTION, √ returns only the nonnegative root: f(9) = 3, full stop.
Functions give one output per input — √ picks the principal one.

options.feedback: Right — the principal root only; a function returns one value.
±3 solves the EQUATION x² = 9 — the function √ picks only the nonnegative root: 3.
The √ symbol never outputs a negative — that's what makes it a function.
That squares the input — the root asks what squares TO 9: f(9) = 3.

widget.prompt: f(x) = √x climbs from f(0) = 0 to f(100) = 10. How much does it climb from x = 100 to x = 400 — that is, what is f(400) − f(100)?

commonErrors.feedback: That's the INPUT gap — the outputs climb only from 10 to √400 = 20: a rise of 10.

widget.fallbackFeedback: √400 = 20, so the rise is 20 − 10 = 10 — three hundred more input for the same ten of output.

explanationVariants: Outputs are principal roots: 0 and up. Range y ≥ 0.
The graph never dips below the x-axis.

widget.prompt: What is the RANGE of f(x) = √x?

options.label: y ≥ 0
options.feedback: Right — every output is a nonnegative principal root.

options.label: all real numbers
options.feedback: That describes the DOMAIN of an odd root — √'s outputs are principal roots, never below 0.

options.label: y > 0
options.feedback: f(0) = 0 is on the graph — zero itself is included: y ≥ 0.

options.label: y ≥ 1
options.feedback: Inputs between 0 and 1 give outputs between 0 and 1 — e.g. f(¼) = ½.

explanationVariants: f(−9) would need √(−9) — not a real number, so no point exists at x = −9.
Negative inputs fall outside the domain entirely.

widget.prompt: Which point is NOT on the graph of f(x) = √x?

options.feedback: Right — x = −9 isn't in the domain; the graph has no points left of the y-axis.
√0 = 0: the graph starts exactly at the origin.

options.label: (¼, ½)
options.feedback: √(¼) = ½ — fractional inputs work fine (and outputs can be small).

explanationVariants: √x reaches 12 when x = 144 — the input must square the target.

widget.prompt: For f(x) = √x, at what input does the output reach 12?

commonErrors.feedback: Doubling won't do it — the input must be the SQUARE of the output: 12² = 144.
6 is 12 halved — going backward through √ means squaring: 144.

steps.body: √x: starts at the origin, first quadrant only, ever slower.
takeaways: Domain x ≥ 0 (no negatives under the root), range y ≥ 0 (principal roots).
The function √ returns ONE value; the equation x² = k has two.
steps.teaser: Next: shifting the start — domains of √(x − 3) and friends.

concept.body: One input, one principal-root output. f(x) = √x at x = 25: what number squares to 25 (taking the nonnegative one)?

commonErrors.feedback: √25 asks what SQUARES to 25 — it isn't 25 ÷ 2.
That's 25² — the root runs the other direction: 5.
